notes:
1. Bhagat Singh — Overview

  • Bhagat Singh was one of the most influential revolutionary nationalists of the Indian freedom struggle.

He combined anti-colonial revolutionary action with:

  • Socialism.
  • Secularism.
  • Anti-communalism.
  • Workers' and peasants' rights.
  • Intellectual criticism of imperialism.
  • He became a national martyr after his execution in 1931.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhagat Singh → HSRA + Saunders Case + Assembly Bombing + Lahore Conspiracy Case

2. Birth

  • Bhagat Singh was born on 28 September 1907.
  • He was born at Banga in Lyallpur district of Punjab in British India.
  • The place is now in Pakistan.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhagat Singh → 28 September 1907 → Banga, Lyallpur

3. Family

  • Bhagat Singh belonged to a politically active Sikh family.
  • Several members of his family were associated with anti-British activity.

4. Father

  • His father was Kishan Singh.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhagat Singh's Father → Kishan Singh

5. Mother

  • His mother was Vidyavati.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhagat Singh's Mother → Vidyavati

6. Ajit Singh

  • Bhagat Singh's uncle Ajit Singh was an important anti-colonial nationalist.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ajit Singh → Uncle of Bhagat Singh

7. Swaran Singh

  • Another uncle, Swaran Singh, was also connected with nationalist politics.

8. Political Environment

Bhagat Singh grew up in an atmosphere shaped by:

  • Punjab agrarian agitation.
  • Ghadar revolutionary traditions.
  • Jallianwala Bagh.
  • Non-Cooperation.
  • Revolutionary nationalism.

9. Ghadar Influence

  • The Ghadar movement strongly influenced revolutionary politics in Punjab.
  • Bhagat Singh admired Ghadar martyrs.

10. Kartar Singh Sarabha

  • Kartar Singh Sarabha was one of Bhagat Singh's revolutionary heroes.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kartar Singh Sarabha → Major Inspiration for Bhagat Singh

11. Jallianwala Bagh

  • The Jallianwala Bagh massacre occurred on 13 April 1919.
  • Bhagat Singh was still a child.
📌 Must-Memorise

Jallianwala Bagh → 1919 → Major Influence on Bhagat Singh's Generation

12. Visit to Jallianwala Bagh

  • Popular accounts state that the young Bhagat Singh visited the massacre site and collected blood-stained earth.
  • The episode became part of his remembered revolutionary biography.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Treat This as a Widely Recounted Biographical Tradition

13. School Education

  • Bhagat Singh studied initially in Punjab.
  • His family avoided institutions regarded as strongly loyal to colonial rule.

14. National College, Lahore

  • Bhagat Singh studied at the National College in Lahore.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhagat Singh → National College, Lahore

15. Founder of National College

  • National College at Lahore was associated with nationalist educational efforts promoted by Lala Lajpat Rai.
📌 Must-Memorise

National College Lahore → Lala Lajpat Rai

16. Nationalist Education

The college encouraged study of:

  • Indian history.
  • National politics.
  • Revolutionary movements.
  • Anti-colonial thought.

17. Bhagat Singh as Reader

  • Bhagat Singh was an avid reader.

He studied:

  • History.
  • Political philosophy.
  • Socialism.
  • Revolutionary movements.
  • European political thought.

18. Languages

He worked with material in languages including:

  • Punjabi.
  • Urdu.
  • Hindi.
  • English.

19. Non-Cooperation Movement

  • Gandhi launched the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1920.
  • The movement strongly influenced young nationalists such as Bhagat Singh.

20. Chauri Chaura

  • Gandhi suspended Non-Cooperation after the Chauri Chaura incident of 1922.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chauri Chaura → 1922 → Non-Cooperation Withdrawn

21. Impact on Young Revolutionaries

  • The withdrawal disappointed many young nationalists.
  • Some moved toward revolutionary organisations.

22. Bhagat Singh's Political Development

His political thought evolved from:

  • Romantic revolutionary nationalism.

toward:

  • Organised socialist revolutionary politics.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bhagat Singh → Revolutionary Nationalism → Socialist Revolutionary Thought

23. Hindustan Republican Association

  • The Hindustan Republican Association, or HRA, was formed in the 1920s.
📌 Must-Memorise

HRA → Hindustan Republican Association

24. Founders/Leaders of HRA

Important leaders included:

  • Ram Prasad Bismil.
  • Sachindra Nath Sanyal.
  • Jogesh Chandra Chatterjee.

25. HRA Objective

  • The HRA sought to overthrow British rule through revolutionary action and establish a republican political order.

26. Kakori Action

  • HRA revolutionaries carried out the Kakori train action on 9 August 1925.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kakori → 9 August 1925

27. Kakori Leaders

Important revolutionaries included:

  • Ram Prasad Bismil.
  • Ashfaqulla Khan.
  • Rajendra Lahiri.
  • Roshan Singh.
  • Chandrashekhar Azad.

28. Kakori Objective

  • Revolutionaries seized government treasury money being transported by train.
  • The goal was to finance revolutionary activities.

29. Kakori Repression

  • British authorities arrested many HRA members.
  • Several leaders were executed.

30. Impact on Revolutionary Movement

  • The Kakori repression severely weakened the HRA.
  • Younger revolutionaries later reorganised it.

31. Bhagat Singh and HRA

  • Bhagat Singh became connected with the revolutionary network that developed from the HRA.

32. Chandrashekhar Azad

  • Chandrashekhar Azad became one of Bhagat Singh's most important revolutionary associates.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhagat Singh + Chandrashekhar Azad → HSRA

33. Naujawan Bharat Sabha

  • Bhagat Singh helped establish the Naujawan Bharat Sabha at Lahore in 1926.
📌 Must-Memorise

Naujawan Bharat Sabha → 1926 → Bhagat Singh

34. Meaning

  • Naujawan Bharat Sabha means broadly "Young India Association."

35. Purpose

The organisation sought to mobilise:

  • Youth.
  • Workers.
  • Peasants.
  • Students.

against:

  • Imperialism.
  • Communalism.

36. Secular Character

  • The Naujawan Bharat Sabha strongly opposed communal divisions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Naujawan Bharat Sabha → Youth + Secular Anti-Imperialism

37. Political Education

The Sabha organised:

  • Meetings.
  • Lectures.
  • Political campaigns.

38. HSRA

  • In 1928, the Hindustan Republican Association was reorganised as the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association.
📌 Must-Memorise

HRA → HSRA → 1928

39. Full Form

HSRA → Hindustan Socialist Republican Association.

40. Socialist Addition

  • The addition of "Socialist" reflected a stronger commitment to social and economic revolution.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

HSRA → Independence + Socialism

41. Feroz Shah Kotla

  • Revolutionary leaders met at Feroz Shah Kotla in Delhi in September 1928 to reorganise the movement.
📌 Must-Memorise

HSRA Reorganisation → Feroz Shah Kotla → 1928

42. Important HSRA Leaders

Important figures included:

  • Bhagat Singh.
  • Chandrashekhar Azad.
  • Sukhdev Thapar.
  • Shivaram Rajguru.
  • Bhagwati Charan Vohra.
  • Yashpal.
  • Batukeshwar Dutt.

43. Objective of HSRA

HSRA sought:

  • End of British imperialism.
  • Establishment of a socialist republican system.
  • Social and economic equality.

44. Simon Commission

  • The Simon Commission arrived in India in 1928.
  • It had no Indian member.
📌 Must-Memorise

Simon Commission → All-White Commission

45. Nationwide Opposition

The slogan became:

  • Simon Go Back.

46. Lahore Protest

  • Lala Lajpat Rai led a major protest against the Simon Commission at Lahore on 30 October 1928.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lajpat Rai → Simon Protest → Lahore → 1928

47. Police Lathi Charge

  • Police used a lathi charge against the demonstrators.

48. James A. Scott

  • Superintendent of Police James A. Scott was blamed by revolutionaries for ordering the lathi charge.
📌 Must-Memorise

Scott → Target Chosen by Revolutionaries

49. Lala Lajpat Rai's Death

  • Lala Lajpat Rai died on 17 November 1928.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lajpat Rai → Died 17 November 1928

50. Punjab Kesari

  • Lala Lajpat Rai was popularly known as Punjab Kesari.

51. Revolutionary Response

  • Bhagat Singh and associates decided to avenge Lala Lajpat Rai's death.

52. Intended Target

  • Their intended target was James A. Scott.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Intended Target → Scott

Actual Victim → J.P. Saunders

53. J.P. Saunders

  • Assistant Superintendent of Police John P. Saunders was mistakenly identified as the intended target.

54. Saunders Assassination

  • Saunders was killed at Lahore on 17 December 1928.
📌 Must-Memorise

Saunders Case → 17 December 1928 → Lahore

55. Rajguru

  • Shivaram Rajguru fired at Saunders during the attack.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rajguru → Saunders Action

56. Bhagat Singh

  • Bhagat Singh also fired during the attack.

57. Chandrashekhar Azad

  • Chandrashekhar Azad provided protection during the operation and escape.

58. Chanan Singh

  • Police constable Chanan Singh pursued the revolutionaries and was shot by Chandrashekhar Azad.

59. Sukhdev

  • Sukhdev was a major organiser within the revolutionary network connected with the Saunders operation.

60. Escape from Lahore

  • Bhagat Singh escaped from Lahore after the assassination.

61. Disguise

  • To avoid recognition, Bhagat Singh cut his hair and beard and changed his appearance.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bhagat Singh → Changed Appearance After Saunders Case

62. Durga Devi Vohra

  • Durga Devi Vohra, popularly known as Durga Bhabhi, helped Bhagat Singh escape from Lahore.
📌 Must-Memorise

Durga Bhabhi → Helped Bhagat Singh Escape

63. Escape Strategy

  • Durga Bhabhi posed as Bhagat Singh's wife during part of the journey.

64. Bhagwati Charan Vohra

  • Durga Bhabhi's husband Bhagwati Charan Vohra was an important HSRA revolutionary.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhagwati Charan Vohra → HSRA

65. Assembly Bomb Plan

  • HSRA later planned a dramatic political action inside the Central Legislative Assembly.

66. Objective of Assembly Bombing

  • The aim was not indiscriminate killing.

The revolutionaries wanted to:

  • Protest repressive legislation.
  • Attract public attention.
  • Use the trial as political propaganda.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Assembly Bombing → Propaganda by Deed, Not Mass Killing

67. Central Legislative Assembly

  • The bombing occurred in Delhi on 8 April 1929.
📌 Must-Memorise

Central Assembly Bombing → 8 April 1929

68. Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt

  • Bhagat Singh carried out the action with Batukeshwar Dutt.
📌 Must-Memorise

Assembly Bombing → Bhagat Singh + Batukeshwar Dutt

69. Bills Being Opposed

The action was associated with opposition to measures such as:

  • Public Safety Bill.
  • Trade Disputes Bill.
📌 Must-Memorise

Assembly Bombing → Public Safety + Trade Disputes Legislation

70. Low-Intensity Bombs

  • Bombs were deliberately thrown into a relatively empty part of the chamber to minimise casualties.

71. Leaflets

  • Revolutionary leaflets were thrown inside the Assembly.

72. Slogan

Bhagat Singh and Dutt shouted:

  • Inquilab Zindabad.
📌 Must-Memorise

Inquilab Zindabad → Bhagat Singh's Revolutionary Movement

73. Meaning

  • Inquilab Zindabad means "Long Live the Revolution."

74. Origin of Slogan

  • The slogan had earlier been used by Urdu poet and political activist Maulana Hasrat Mohani.
  • Bhagat Singh and his comrades made it enormously popular.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Bhagat Singh Popularised "Inquilab Zindabad"

He Did Not Necessarily Coin It

75. "Down with Imperialism"

  • Another slogan associated with the revolutionary action was "Down with Imperialism."

76. Deliberate Arrest

  • Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt did not attempt to escape after the Assembly bombing.
📌 Must-Memorise

Assembly Bombing → Deliberate Surrender

77. Purpose of Surrender

They wanted to use:

  • Court proceedings.
  • Newspapers.
  • Prison protest.

to communicate revolutionary ideas.

78. Arrest

  • Both were arrested immediately.

79. Assembly Bomb Case

  • They were tried for the Assembly bombing.

80. Sentence

  • Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt received life transportation/imprisonment in the Assembly Bomb Case.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Death Sentence Came from Lahore Conspiracy Case, Not Assembly Bomb Case

81. Lahore Conspiracy Investigation

  • During investigation, police connected Bhagat Singh with the Saunders assassination.

82. Lahore Conspiracy Case

  • Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, Sukhdev and other revolutionaries were prosecuted in the Lahore Conspiracy Case.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lahore Conspiracy Case → Saunders Assassination

83. Prison Conditions

  • Indian political prisoners complained of discriminatory prison treatment compared with European prisoners.

84. Hunger Strike

  • Bhagat Singh and other revolutionaries launched a prolonged hunger strike in jail.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhagat Singh → Hunger Strike for Political Prisoner Rights

85. Main Demands

They demanded:

  • Better food.
  • Reading materials.
  • Newspapers.
  • Equal treatment.
  • No degrading labour.
  • Recognition as political prisoners.

86. Political Prisoner Status

  • The strike transformed prison conditions into a national political issue.

87. Jatin Das

  • Jatindranath Das, commonly called Jatin Das, joined the hunger strike.
📌 Must-Memorise

Jatin Das → Lahore Jail Hunger Strike

88. Death of Jatin Das

  • Jatin Das died on 13 September 1929 after a 63-day hunger strike.
📌 Must-Memorise

Jatin Das → Died 13 September 1929 → 63-Day Fast

89. National Reaction

  • Jatin Das's death produced massive public outrage.

90. Funeral Procession

  • His body was taken by train from Lahore to Calcutta.
  • Large crowds gathered along the route.

91. Subhas Chandra Bose

  • Subhas Chandra Bose was among the prominent leaders associated with the reception and funeral mobilisation in Calcutta.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Jatin Das Martyrdom → Nationwide Political Mobilisation

92. Bhagat Singh's Popularity

  • The hunger strike dramatically increased Bhagat Singh's popularity beyond revolutionary circles.

93. Courtroom as Political Platform

Bhagat Singh and his comrades used courtroom statements to explain:

  • Revolution.
  • Socialism.
  • Anti-imperialism.

94. Meaning of Revolution

  • For Bhagat Singh, revolution did not mean merely bomb and pistol actions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhagat Singh's Revolution → Fundamental Social Transformation

95. Social Revolution

He envisioned changes in:

  • Economic relations.
  • Class power.
  • Political institutions.
  • Social inequality.

96. "Bomb and Pistol"

  • Bhagat Singh explicitly argued that revolution could not be reduced to bombs and pistols.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Revolution ≠ Mere Violence

97. Socialism

  • By the late 1920s, Bhagat Singh had become strongly committed to socialist ideas.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhagat Singh → Socialist Revolutionary

98. Workers

  • He believed workers were central to social transformation.

99. Peasants

  • He also saw peasants as a major revolutionary force.

100. Anti-Capitalist Critique

  • Bhagat Singh criticised systems of economic exploitation, whether foreign or indigenous.

101. Independence Beyond British Withdrawal

  • He argued that simply replacing British rulers with Indian elites would not constitute full revolution.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bhagat Singh → Political Independence + Socio-Economic Change

102. Secularism

  • Bhagat Singh strongly opposed communal politics.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhagat Singh → Secular + Anti-Communal

103. Communalism

  • He regarded communal conflict as a serious obstacle to workers' and people's unity.

104. Religion and Politics

  • Bhagat Singh increasingly argued that religion should not divide the political struggle.

105. Why I Am an Atheist

  • Bhagat Singh wrote the famous essay Why I Am an Atheist in prison in 1930.
📌 Must-Memorise

Why I Am an Atheist → Bhagat Singh → 1930

106. Context of Essay

  • The essay responded partly to claims that Bhagat Singh's atheism reflected vanity or arrogance.

107. Nature of His Atheism

His atheism emerged from:

  • Rational inquiry.
  • Political thought.
  • Critical reflection.

108. Rationalism

Bhagat Singh valued:

  • Reason.
  • Critical thinking.
  • Intellectual independence.

109. "To Young Political Workers"

  • Bhagat Singh wrote an important political document commonly known as To Young Political Workers.
📌 Must-Memorise

To Young Political Workers → Bhagat Singh

110. Themes

It discussed:

  • Revolution.
  • Political organisation.
  • Workers.
  • Peasants.
  • Socialism.

111. Study in Prison

  • Bhagat Singh continued intensive reading while imprisoned.

112. Prison Notebook

  • Notes from his prison reading survive in what is commonly called his Jail Notebook or Prison Notebook.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bhagat Singh → Jail Notebook

113. Authors Read

His reading included thinkers and writers associated with:

  • Marxism.
  • Socialism.
  • Revolution.
  • Literature.
  • Philosophy.

114. Karl Marx

  • Bhagat Singh studied Marxist political thought.

115. Lenin

  • He also read works associated with Vladimir Lenin and the Russian Revolution.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhagat Singh → Marx + Lenin Influence

116. Lenin Memorial Tradition

  • Popular accounts state that Bhagat Singh was reading about Lenin shortly before his execution.
  • This became an enduring part of his revolutionary memory.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Use as Widely Recounted Tradition Rather Than Over-Specific Proven Detail

117. International Revolutionary Thought

Bhagat Singh studied revolutionary movements beyond India to understand:

  • Imperialism.
  • Class struggle.
  • Republicanism.

118. French Revolution

  • Ideas from the French Revolution and European revolutionary history formed part of the intellectual world of young Indian revolutionaries.

119. Russian Revolution

  • The Russian Revolution of 1917 strongly influenced socialist revolutionary thinking globally, including Indian youth.

120. HSRA's Socialist Objective

  • The HSRA increasingly envisaged a socialist republic rather than merely transfer of political power.

121. Republicanism

  • Bhagat Singh rejected monarchy and hereditary political authority.

122. Exploitation

His revolutionary goal opposed exploitation:

  • By one nation over another.
  • By one class over another.

123. Mass Politics

  • Bhagat Singh increasingly recognised that lasting revolution required organised mass participation.

124. Trade Unions

  • He regarded workers' organisation as important to political transformation.

125. Peasant Organisation

  • He also emphasised the political organisation of peasants.

126. Youth Politics

  • Naujawan Bharat Sabha represented his effort to politically educate young people outside purely secret revolutionary activity.

127. Propaganda vs Terror

  • Bhagat Singh's later writings distinguished revolutionary political education from individual acts of terror.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Do Not Describe Mature Bhagat Singh's Politics as Only "Terrorism"

128. Special Tribunal

  • The British government established a special tribunal for the Lahore Conspiracy Case.

129. Lahore Conspiracy Case Ordinance

  • A special ordinance altered the normal judicial process and facilitated an accelerated trial.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lahore Case → Special Tribunal

130. Defence and Boycott

  • Bhagat Singh and other accused sometimes challenged or boycotted aspects of the proceedings.

131. Death Sentence

  • Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev were sentenced to death.
📌 Must-Memorise

Death Sentence → Bhagat Singh + Rajguru + Sukhdev

132. Popular Trio

The three became remembered together as:

  • Bhagat Singh.
  • Rajguru.
  • Sukhdev.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhagat Singh–Rajguru–Sukhdev → 23 March 1931

133. Appeals for Commutation

  • Political leaders and members of the public appealed for commutation of the death sentences.

134. Gandhi–Irwin Period

  • The execution issue became politically important during the period of the Gandhi–Irwin Pact in 1931.

135. Gandhi's Position

  • Gandhi raised the question of clemency with Viceroy Lord Irwin.
  • He did not obtain commutation of the sentences.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Claims that Gandhi "ordered" or "wanted" the execution are historically inaccurate.

136. Gandhi–Irwin Pact

  • The Gandhi–Irwin Pact was signed on 5 March 1931.

137. Execution Date

  • Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev were executed on 23 March 1931.
📌 Must-Memorise

23 March 1931 → Bhagat Singh + Rajguru + Sukhdev Executed

138. Place of Execution

  • They were executed in Lahore Central Jail.
📌 Must-Memorise

Execution → Lahore Central Jail

139. Scheduled Date

  • The executions were carried out earlier than the publicly expected timing on the following day.

140. Cremation

  • Their bodies were secretly taken toward the Sutlej River area and cremated.

141. Hussainiwala

  • Hussainiwala, near the India–Pakistan border in Punjab, became associated with their martyrdom memorial.
📌 Must-Memorise

Hussainiwala → Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, Sukhdev Memorial

142. Shaheed Diwas

  • 23 March is widely observed as Shaheed Diwas or Martyrs' Day in memory of Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev.
📌 Must-Memorise

23 March → Shaheed Diwas

143. Different Martyrs' Day Dates — Trap

  • 30 January → Martyrs' Day associated nationally with Gandhi.
  • 23 March → Shaheed Diwas associated with Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite Trap

Do Not Interchange 30 January and 23 March

144. Rajguru

  • Shivaram Hari Rajguru was from Maharashtra.
  • He was a skilled revolutionary marksman.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rajguru → Maharashtra

145. Sukhdev

  • Sukhdev Thapar was a major revolutionary organiser from Punjab.
  • He was closely associated with HSRA.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sukhdev → Punjab → HSRA Organiser

146. Batukeshwar Dutt

  • Batukeshwar Dutt participated with Bhagat Singh in the Central Legislative Assembly bombing.
📌 Must-Memorise

Batukeshwar Dutt → Assembly Bombing

147. Batukeshwar Dutt's Fate

  • Dutt was sentenced to transportation for life rather than executed in the Lahore Conspiracy Case.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Assembly Bombing Pair → Bhagat Singh + Dutt

Execution Trio → Bhagat Singh + Rajguru + Sukhdev

148. Chandrashekhar Azad

  • Chandrashekhar Azad remained a central HSRA leader after Bhagat Singh's arrest.

149. Alfred Park

  • Chandrashekhar Azad died in a gun battle with police at Alfred Park in Allahabad on 27 February 1931.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chandrashekhar Azad → Alfred Park → 27 February 1931

150. Present Name

  • Alfred Park is now known as Chandrashekhar Azad Park.

151. Bhagwati Charan Vohra

  • Bhagwati Charan Vohra was a major HSRA ideologue and organiser.

152. Philosophy of the Bomb

  • Bhagwati Charan Vohra is associated with the revolutionary pamphlet The Philosophy of the Bomb.
📌 Must-Memorise

The Philosophy of the Bomb → Bhagwati Charan Vohra

153. Death of Vohra

  • Bhagwati Charan Vohra died in 1930 while testing a bomb near the Ravi River.

154. Durga Bhabhi

  • Durga Devi Vohra participated actively in revolutionary networks.
  • She was not merely a passive helper.
📌 Must-Memorise

Durga Bhabhi → Woman Revolutionary of HSRA Network

155. Women in Revolutionary Movement

Women associated with revolutionary nationalism contributed through:

  • Shelter.
  • Transport.
  • Intelligence.
  • Fundraising.
  • Direct action.

156. Bhagat Singh and Journalism

  • Bhagat Singh contributed to newspapers and political publications under different names.

157. Kirti

  • He was associated with the Punjabi journal Kirti.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kirti → Bhagat Singh's Political Writing

158. Kirti Kisan Party Context

  • Kirti reflected radical worker-peasant politics in Punjab.

159. Pratap

  • Bhagat Singh also worked for or contributed to nationalist publications such as Pratap.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bhagat Singh → Revolutionary Journalism

160. Ganesh Shankar Vidyarthi

  • Journalist and nationalist Ganesh Shankar Vidyarthi influenced and assisted young revolutionaries including Bhagat Singh.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ganesh Shankar Vidyarthi → Journalist + Nationalist Mentor Figure

161. Pratap Newspaper

  • Ganesh Shankar Vidyarthi was closely associated with the newspaper Pratap.
📌 Must-Memorise

Pratap → Ganesh Shankar Vidyarthi

162. Anti-Communalism of Vidyarthi

  • Ganesh Shankar Vidyarthi died in 1931 while trying to protect people during communal violence in Kanpur.

163. Revolutionary Organisations — Distinction

HRA:

  • Earlier organisation.
  • Republican objective.

HSRA:

  • Reorganised in 1928.
  • Explicit socialist orientation.
📌 Must-Memorise

HRA → HSRA → Socialist Shift

164. Kakori vs Saunders

Kakori:

1925.

  • HRA.
  • Government train treasury.

Saunders:

1928.

  • HSRA circle.
  • Lahore.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Do Not Mix the Two Cases

165. Saunders vs Assembly Bombing

Saunders:

  • 17 December 1928.
  • Lahore.
  • Retaliatory assassination.

Assembly Bombing:

  • 8 April 1929.
  • Delhi.
  • Political demonstration.

166. Assembly Bombing vs Lahore Case

  • Assembly Bomb Case produced a life sentence.
  • Lahore Conspiracy Case produced the death sentence.
📌 Must-Memorise

Death Sentence → Lahore Conspiracy Case

167. Bhagat Singh's Nationalism

  • Bhagat Singh opposed British imperial rule absolutely.
  • He also believed nationalism should move toward a socially just republic.

168. Socialist Republic

  • The HSRA's ultimate political ideal was a socialist republican order.

169. Meaning of Independence

For Bhagat Singh, independence meant more than:

  • Replacing British officials with Indian officials.

It required ending:

  • Exploitation.
  • Class domination.
  • Imperialism.

170. Revolution and Democracy

  • His writings increasingly emphasised political consciousness and organised mass action rather than adventurism alone.

171. Revolutionary Violence

  • Bhagat Singh accepted revolutionary violence in particular political situations.
  • However, his mature political thought cannot be reduced to violence.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Bhagat Singh → Revolutionary Thinker, Not Merely an Armed Activist

172. Capital Punishment and Martyrdom

  • The colonial government's execution of the three young revolutionaries turned them into powerful symbols of anti-imperial resistance.

173. Youth Appeal

Bhagat Singh became especially influential among:

  • Students.
  • Young workers.
  • Radical Congress supporters.
  • Socialist nationalists.

174. Popular Name

  • He is widely remembered as Shaheed Bhagat Singh.
📌 Must-Memorise

Shaheed-e-Azam → Popular Honorific Associated with Bhagat Singh

175. "Shaheed-e-Azam"

  • The honorific Shaheed-e-Azam, meaning "great martyr," is commonly associated with Bhagat Singh.

176. Turbaned vs Hat Image

  • Photographs of Bhagat Singh in both Sikh appearance and a felt hat have become iconic.
  • The hat portrait especially became a symbol of his modern revolutionary identity.

177. Secular Revolutionary Identity

  • Cutting his hair to evade the police was a practical revolutionary decision.
  • It should not be simplistically treated as a rejection of his family or cultural roots.

178. Atheism vs Secularism

  • Bhagat Singh personally became an atheist.
  • Politically, he advocated secular unity against communalism.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Personal Atheism + Political Secularism → Distinct but Related

179. Religion and Revolution

  • He criticised the use of religion to divide people politically.

180. Communal Riots

  • Communal tensions in the 1920s strengthened his conviction that class and national unity had to overcome religious divisions.

181. Language Question

  • Bhagat Singh also reflected on language and script issues in Punjab.
  • He supported communication that could reach ordinary people rather than linguistic sectarianism.

182. Peasants and Workers

His later political programme increasingly focused on:

  • Organisation of peasants.
  • Organisation of workers.
  • Social transformation.

183. Labour Legislation Context

  • The Trade Disputes Bill opposed by the Assembly bombers was seen as restricting labour organisation and strikes.

184. Public Safety Bill

  • The Public Safety Bill was associated with colonial attempts to restrict radical political activity.

185. "To Make the Deaf Hear"

  • The Assembly bombing leaflets used the idea that a loud noise was necessary "to make the deaf hear."
📌 Must-Memorise

"To Make the Deaf Hear" → Assembly Bombing Political Message

186. French Revolutionary Connection

  • The phrase was associated with earlier European revolutionary rhetoric and was adopted by the HSRA.

187. Deliberate Non-Lethal Intent

  • The location and strength of the bombs were selected to avoid mass casualties.

188. Court Statements

  • The revolutionaries openly accepted responsibility for the Assembly action while explaining its political purpose.

189. Colonial Repression

  • The government used the cases to dismantle revolutionary networks across northern India.

190. Approvers

  • Police investigations relied partly on testimony from former associates who became government witnesses.

191. Hans Raj Vohra

  • Hans Raj Vohra became an approver in the Lahore Conspiracy Case.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hans Raj Vohra → Government Witness in Lahore Case

192. Jai Gopal

  • Jai Gopal also became a prosecution witness in the Saunders investigation.

193. Revolutionary Secrecy

  • The use of underground cells made the movement difficult to penetrate initially but vulnerable when members were arrested.

194. Public Sympathy

  • By 1930–31, Bhagat Singh's public standing extended well beyond Punjab.

195. Congress Karachi Session

  • The Karachi Congress met shortly after the execution of Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev in March 1931.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Karachi Congress 1931 → Immediately After Execution

196. Congress Tribute

  • Congress leaders expressed admiration for the courage and sacrifice of the executed revolutionaries while maintaining disagreement with political violence.

197. Gandhi and Revolutionary Youth

  • Gandhi rejected violence but acknowledged the bravery and patriotism of young revolutionaries.

198. Bhagat Singh vs Gandhi

Gandhi:

  • Non-violent Satyagraha.

Bhagat Singh:

  • Revolutionary socialism and selective armed action.

Both:

  • Sought the end of British rule.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Different Methods ≠ Different Goal of Ending Colonialism

Bhagat Singh:

  • HSRA.
  • Executed in 1931.

Subhas Bose:

  • Congress president.
  • Forward Bloc.
  • INA during World War II.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Bhagat Singh Was Not an INA Leader

Chandrashekhar Azad:

Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected

When was Bhagat Singh born? → 28 September 1907.

Where was he born? → Banga, Lyallpur district, Punjab.

Where is that place today? → Pakistan.

Who was Bhagat Singh's father? → Kishan Singh.

Who was his mother? → Vidyavati.

Which nationalist uncle influenced his family environment? → Ajit Singh.

Which Ghadar revolutionary deeply inspired Bhagat Singh? → Kartar Singh Sarabha.

Which 1919 event strongly influenced his generation? → Jallianwala Bagh massacre.

Where did Bhagat Singh study? → National College, Lahore.

Who was associated with establishing National College? → Lala Lajpat Rai.

Which Gandhian movement influenced Bhagat Singh as a youth? → Non-Cooperation Movement.

Which incident led Gandhi to suspend it? → Chauri Chaura, 1922.

What was HRA? → Hindustan Republican Association.

Name major HRA leaders. → Ram Prasad Bismil, Sachindra Nath Sanyal and others.

Which famous revolutionary action did HRA conduct in 1925? → Kakori train action.

Was Bhagat Singh a participant in Kakori? → No.

Which youth organisation did Bhagat Singh help found? → Naujawan Bharat Sabha.

When? → 1926.

Where? → Lahore.

What did it oppose? → Imperialism and communalism.

What did HRA become in 1928? → Hindustan Socialist Republican Association.

What does HSRA stand for? → Hindustan Socialist Republican Association.

Where was HSRA reorganised? → Feroz Shah Kotla, Delhi.

Why was "Socialist" added? → To emphasise socio-economic revolution and a socialist republic.

Name major HSRA leaders. → Bhagat Singh, Chandrashekhar Azad, Sukhdev, Rajguru, Bhagwati Charan Vohra and others.

Which British commission caused nationwide protest in 1928? → Simon Commission.

Why was it opposed? → It had no Indian member.

Who led the Lahore protest against it? → Lala Lajpat Rai.

On what date? → 30 October 1928.

Who was blamed for ordering the lathi charge? → James A. Scott.

When did Lala Lajpat Rai die? → 17 November 1928.

Who did the revolutionaries intend to assassinate? → James A. Scott.

Who was actually killed? → J.P. Saunders.

When? → 17 December 1928.

Where? → Lahore.

Who participated prominently? → Bhagat Singh and Rajguru, with Chandrashekhar Azad providing support.

Who helped Bhagat Singh escape Lahore? → Durga Devi Vohra, or Durga Bhabhi.

Why did Bhagat Singh cut his hair and beard? → To avoid police identification during escape.

Who was Durga Bhabhi's husband? → Bhagwati Charan Vohra.

Which political action did Bhagat Singh carry out in Delhi? → Central Legislative Assembly bombing.

Date? → 8 April 1929.

Who accompanied him? → Batukeshwar Dutt.

Which proposed measures were being opposed? → Public Safety Bill and Trade Disputes legislation.

Were the bombs intended to kill large numbers of people? → No.

What was the purpose? → Dramatic political protest and public propaganda against colonial repression.

Which slogan was shouted? → Inquilab Zindabad.

What does it mean? → Long Live the Revolution.

Did Bhagat Singh originally coin the slogan? → It had earlier usage, notably associated with Hasrat Mohani; Bhagat Singh and his comrades popularised it enormously.

Did Bhagat Singh and Dutt escape after bombing? → No.

Why? → They deliberately surrendered to use the court as a political platform.

Which slogan accompanied their anti-colonial message? → Down with Imperialism.

What sentence did Bhagat Singh receive in the Assembly Bomb Case? → Life imprisonment/transportation.

Which case eventually brought the death sentence? → Lahore Conspiracy Case.

What was that case primarily connected with? → Saunders assassination and HSRA revolutionary activities.

Why did Bhagat Singh undertake a hunger strike? → To demand fair treatment and political-prisoner rights.

What were the demands? → Better food, reading material, newspapers, exemption from degrading labour and equal prison treatment.

Who became the most famous martyr of the hunger strike? → Jatin Das.

How long did Jatin Das fast? → 63 days.

When did he die? → 13 September 1929.

What effect did his death have? → It created nationwide outrage and sympathy for political prisoners.

What did Bhagat Singh mean by revolution? → Fundamental political, social and economic transformation, not simply bomb and pistol actions.

Which ideology increasingly shaped his mature thought? → Socialism.

Did Bhagat Singh support communal politics? → No.

What was his position? → Strongly secular and anti-communal.

Which famous essay did he write in jail? → Why I Am an Atheist.

When? → 1930.

What did it reflect? → Rationalism, critical inquiry and his personal atheism.

Which other political document is associated with him? → To Young Political Workers.

What issues did it address? → Revolution, socialism, workers, peasants and political organisation.

What is Bhagat Singh's Jail Notebook? → Notes and quotations from his extensive prison reading.

Which socialist thinkers influenced him? → Marx, Lenin and wider socialist literature.

Did Bhagat Singh want only transfer of power from British elites to Indian elites? → No.

What did he seek? → Political freedom accompanied by an end to social and economic exploitation.

Who were sentenced to death with Bhagat Singh? → Shivaram Rajguru and Sukhdev Thapar.

When were they executed? → 23 March 1931.

Where? → Lahore Central Jail.

What is observed on 23 March? → Shaheed Diwas in memory of Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev.

Which place is associated with their martyr memorial? → Hussainiwala.

What is the difference between 23 March and 30 January? → 23 March commemorates Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev; 30 January is Martyrs' Day associated with Gandhi's assassination.

Who was Rajguru? → Maharashtra-born HSRA revolutionary executed with Bhagat Singh.

Who was Sukhdev? → Punjab-based HSRA organiser executed with Bhagat Singh.

Who was Batukeshwar Dutt? → Bhagat Singh's partner in the Assembly bombing.

Was Dutt executed with Bhagat Singh? → No.

Who was Chandrashekhar Azad? → Senior HSRA revolutionary leader.

Where did Azad die? → Alfred Park, Allahabad.

When? → 27 February 1931.

What is the park now called? → Chandrashekhar Azad Park.

Who wrote The Philosophy of the Bomb? → Bhagwati Charan Vohra.

Who was Ganesh Shankar Vidyarthi? → Nationalist journalist who assisted revolutionary youth and was associated with Pratap.

Which publication was Bhagat Singh associated with in Punjab? → Kirti.

What is the difference between HRA and HSRA? → HRA was the earlier republican revolutionary body; HSRA added an explicit socialist objective in 1928.

What is the difference between Kakori and Saunders? → Kakori was an HRA train-treasury action in 1925; Saunders was killed by HSRA revolutionaries at Lahore in 1928.

What is the difference between Saunders case and Assembly bombing? → Saunders was a targeted assassination in Lahore; Assembly bombing was a deliberately demonstrative political action in Delhi.

What is the most important ideological fact about Bhagat Singh? → He evolved into a socialist, secular, rationalist revolutionary who believed independence required the removal of both imperialism and socio-economic exploitation.

What is the central TNPSC takeaway? → Bhagat Singh transformed revolutionary nationalism from individual anti-British action toward an explicitly socialist, secular and mass-oriented revolutionary vision; the Saunders case, Assembly bombing, prison hunger strike and his execution with Rajguru and Sukhdev on 23 March 1931 made him one of India's greatest revolutionary symbols.
